newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine 1997 avg interest rate seen at 10.6 pct.
newsitem.headline: Philippine 1997 avg interest rate seen at 10.6 pct.

text.p: Philippine interest rates could drop to an average of 10.6 percent in 1997 from a 1996 estimate of 12.4 percent due to cuts in bank reserve requirements planned for next year, a Reuters poll of four banks on Friday showed.
The average interest rate predictions were based on the benchmark 91-day treasury bills.

Despite the planned cut of two percentage points in reserve requirements, the peso is seen weakening only slightly to 26.60 per U.S. dollar on average in 1997 from 26.22 this year, the bank economists said.

The Philippine central bank's decision to ease monetary policy comes as inflation has slowed to single-digit levels. The latest year-on-year inflation was 4.7 percent in October versus 11 percent in the year-ago month.
The bank decided to cut the reserve requirement in two phases, by one percentage point on January 3 and again by another point on July 4.

The move is expected to free up some 13.4 billion pesos ($510 million) in banks and boost total domestic liquidity by 54.8 billion pesos ($2.085 billion), but Central Bank governor Gabriel Singson calmed fears the market would be flooded with cash.
"Monetary authorities will ensure that domestic liquidity is kept within limits and consistent with the inflation target of 6.5 percent in 1997," he said.

Analysts seemed convinced by the assurance. "Interest rates will go down but not as much. The Central Bank won't sacrifice price stability for economic growth," said Paul Joseph Garcia, economist at Metropolitan Bank and Trust Co.
The economists said the fall in interest rates was expected to begin immediately and most expected lower rates at next Monday's weekly treasury bills auction.
By year-end, the 91-day bill rate could drop to 11.5 percent or as low as 11.25 percent from the present 11.70, they said.
By July next year, "it could become single-digit, about nine percent," Emma Pante, economist at Far East Bank said.
With falling interest rates, the peso would fall but by a much smaller margin, participants in the poll said.
The 1997 low for the Philippine currency was seen at between 26.80 and 27 pesos to a dollar from around 26.30 at the start of the year. On Friday, the peso was at 26.288.
The pressure on the peso caused by falling rates and a widening trade deficit was seen offset by higher dollar inflows from foreign direct and portfolio investments.
"The dollar inflows will compensate for the reduction in interest rate differential (versus the U.S. dollar)," Manny Lim, vice president of ING Bank, said.
Economists had earlier predicted the 1997 trade deficit could widen to $13.5 to $14.0 billion from the 1996 estimate of $12 to $12.5 billion due to an expanding economy.
Following are the bank projections for 1997:
avg peso rate (vs dollar) avg 91 day-T-bill
AsianBank 26.70 11.0
Far East Bank 26.70 10.0-10.5
ING Bank 26.50 10.5
Metrobank 26.50 10.6
Conversion US$ = 26.288
